scenes.tts: An axon grows toward the midline of the nervous system. It crosses to the far side. Then it never crosses back. Its neighbours stay on their own side and never cross at all. Here is the puzzle. The midline did not change. The same cells stand there before, during and after the crossing. So what changed? The change has to be in the axon.
scenes.visual: A commissural axon grows to the midline strip, crosses, and a crossed-out arrow blocks the way back; an ipsilateral axon stops short; a question mark rests on the growth cone, which is then circled.
scenes.narration: An axon grows toward the midline of the nervous system. It crosses to the far side. Then it never crosses back. Its neighbours stay on their own side and never cross at all. Here is the puzzle. The midline did not change. The same cells stand there before, during and after the crossing. So what changed? The change has to be in the axon.

scenes.tts: The midline holds a repellent called Slit. The axon carries a receptor for it, called Robo. When Slit binds Robo, the growth cone retreats. Axons that never cross carry Robo from the start. Axons that do cross carry high levels of Robo only after they have crossed. So the crossing axon is deaf to Slit until it is over.
scenes.visual: Red Slit dots around the midline; a growth cone with yellow Robo is pushed back; a second growth cone without Robo passes through and gains Robo on the far side.

scenes.tts: The fly embryo exposed the logic. Its nerve cord looks like a ladder, with rungs where axons cross. Lose Robo, and too many axons cross, and some cross back. Lose a protein called Comm, and almost no axon crosses. Lose both, and the embryo looks like the Robo mutant. Comm works by lowering Robo. Once Robo is gone, losing Comm changes nothing.
scenes.visual: A ladder of two rails and rungs; beside it appear the robo ladder (extra crossings), the comm ladder (no rungs), and the double mutant that matches robo; then a purple Comm chip with an inhibition arrow to a yellow Robo chip.

scenes.tts: Comm works inside the commissural neuron. It is made for a short time, before and during crossing. It meets newly made Robo and diverts it from the road to the surface. Robo ends up in late endosomes and lysosomes, where it is destroyed. Parts of this model are still debated. The axon crosses with no Robo on its tip. Then the neuron stops making Comm. Robo reaches the growth cone, and Slit now repels it.
scenes.visual: A neuron with a road from the cell body to the growth cone; Comm diverts Robo into a lysosome; the bare tip crosses the midline; Comm stops, Robo flows to the tip, and Slit pushes the cone away.

scenes.tts: No vertebrate Comm has been found. Mice use another protein, Robo three. It is made on commissural axons before they cross. It blunts how Robo one and Robo two respond to Slit, while they stay in the membrane. After the axon crosses, Robo three largely disappears. Then Robo one and Robo two are free to respond. Comm destroys the receptor. Robo three silences it.
scenes.visual: A large growth cone with yellow Robo1 and Robo2 under an orange Robo3 cover; Slit dots bounce off while it crosses; the cover fades on the far side and Slit pushes the cone away; Comm destroys, Robo3 silences.

scenes.tts: Both routes give the same result. The axon is deaf to Slit before crossing, and responsive after. So you can predict a midline phenotype. Ask three questions. Is Slit there? Can the axon hear it? And when does it start hearing? An axon that hears Slit too early never crosses. One that never hears it crosses again.
scenes.visual: A timeline deaf then responsive across the midline; then three question chips and two outcome panels: hears too early (stalls, never crosses) and never hears (crosses and returns).
